prize_parts.citation: For the theory of defect-mediated melting of two-dimensional solids and the prediction of the hexatic phase

statement.case_for: Dislocation-mediated melting with an intervening hexatic phase is a compact mechanism: two successive unbinding transitions, controlled by renormalization-group flow, explain a messy many-body problem with a small number of stiffness parameters. It gave concrete, testable predictions, such as the temperature-dependent orientational correlation length and the characteristic exponent at the melting transition. These were later confirmed in colloidal monolayers, liquid-crystal films and simulations, so the theory is understood and has been checked, not only observed to work. It carries the topological-defect idea of Kosterlitz and Thouless from the XY model to elasticity, with consequences for soft matter, thin films and active and driven 2D systems. The attribution is clean: Halperin and Nelson for the two-step scenario and the hexatic phase, Young for the independent and closely related treatment. The theory is more than forty years old and has stood up to repeated experimental and numerical tests, so maturity is not in question.
statement.case_against: B012 has the thinnest opening support in this shortlist (one first-place vote and no other ranking in the union), and several colleagues find the precision-instrument or platform stories more compelling. It is also a conceptual extension of work already honoured in 2016, which invites the objection that the prize would partly recognise a sequel. Numerical and experimental work shows that melting in some 2D systems is first order, or that the two-step scenario depends on the interaction, so the picture is less universal than the textbook version. If the committee wants a discovery with a clear before-and-after in a laboratory, B018 is stronger on that criterion than B012.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B018) are a new way of measuring time: the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts, reaches about 1e-18 uncertainty, and has direct uses in redefining the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of constants. The two-name credit of Katori and Ye is clean.
responses.response: I agree that the credit for B018 is cleaner than for most candidates here, and the magic-wavelength idea is a simple, general mechanism, which is the kind of idea I value. Where I disagree is on how much weight the 1e-18 figure should carry. It is a metrological record built on a tool, and I would ask the committee to separate the lattice concept (Katori) from the accuracy campaign (Ye, with Lemonde, Takamoto and others also in the story). I would not rank B018 below B012 on scientific merit. My difference with you is that I put a theory resolving a long-standing question about how 2D matter melts ahead of a better instrument. I treat B018 as my first alternative and could move to it if we find that the 2D melting prize looks too much like a sequel to 2016.

responses.point: IceCube (B007) opened neutrino astronomy with a cubic-kilometre detector, with a diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068, and the credit should go to Halzen and Karle with Yoshida's role judged less decisive.
responses.response: The science is impressive, but I have a serious reservation about attribution. A detector built and analysed by several hundred people gives no obvious basis for a statutory one-to-three split, and you yourself drop Yoshida, which shows how arbitrary the cut is. I also doubt the source associations are yet mature enough to carry a prize on their own: TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are single-source evidence at modest significance, and the diffuse-flux claim leaves the origin open. I would be more comfortable if the committee could point to one decisive individual contribution beyond the concept and the construction. Until then I rank B007 below B018 and B008, though not below B012 on merit, only on attribution.

responses.point: Tunnel magnetoresistance (B003) is an original experimental discovery with a clear observable and large societal benefit, and the credit should go to the 1995 originators Miyazaki and Moodera rather than also to Parkin.
responses.response: I accept that the experimental priority in 1995 is clear and that the societal benefit is real, so I take B003 seriously. I do not agree with removing Parkin. The step from the 1995 effect of a few tens of percent to the coherent-tunnelling MgO barrier is where the physics became understood, via the symmetry-filtering theory of Butler and Mathon, and a citation that leaves out the larger, understood effect risks crediting the first observation and not the full mechanism. That is also the problem for the three-name form, since Butler and Mathon would be excluded. For me this attribution problem and the technological emphasis place B003 below the clock and circuit QED.

responses.point: Gamma-ray burst afterglows (B038) settled the cosmological origin of GRBs, are mature after twenty-five years, and are arguably overdue, though the boundary of credit between BeppoSAX and the optical and redshift groups is contestable.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of maturity and with the point that recognition is overdue. I would press you on attribution, which you flag yourself. The afterglow localisation, the optical transient and the redshift came from several groups within weeks, so Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni represent a choice among many. A citation such as 'for the discovery of gamma-ray burst afterglows' would hide that choice, and the committee would then have to defend the exclusions. I find B038 a strong discovery with the same attribution difficulty as B007, and I would want a concrete argument for why this triple and not another before I support it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will view the 2D melting theory as a distinct achievement or as a sequel to the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize.
How much weight the first-order melting results and system-dependent behaviour should carry against the claim of a universal two-step scenario.
Whether the historical priority between Halperin-Nelson and Young is as clean as I describe, since I am relying on my own recall of the 1978-1979 papers.

Whether a two-part prize combining a theory (B012) and a precision or platform achievement (B018 or B008) would be better received, given that the three-person limit makes any such pairing costly in names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate. B012 is close to my own statistical-physics field, and I have no recorded link to Young, Halperin or Nelson. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (GU and Chalmers), but no specific collaboration or conflict regarding any shortlisted candidate was found.
